title: RAG vs Fine-tune vs Long-Context
summary: Three techniques inject knowledge or behavior into an LLM, and they solve different problems. RAG retrieves relevant text at query time — best for large, fresh, or citable knowledge. Fine-tuning bakes patterns into the weights — best for style, format, and behavior. Long-context stuffs everything into the prompt — best for a small, stable corpus that fits. The skill is matching the technique to the need, and knowing they combine.

subtopics.title: Three different levers, three different problems
subtopics.explanation: RAG changes what the model can see (retrieved text in the prompt), fine-tuning changes how the model behaves (patterns in the weights), and long-context changes how much the model reads at once (everything in the prompt). They aren't competitors so much as answers to different questions — knowledge vs behavior vs corpus-size. Naming which lever a problem actually needs is the whole decision, and it's the first thing to get right before touching any of them.

subtopics.title: When RAG wins: freshness, scale, and citations
subtopics.explanation: RAG is the default for knowledge that is large, changes often, or must be attributable, because you update an index instead of retraining, and every answer can point at the chunk it came from. It shines when the corpus is far too big to fit any context window and when 'why did it say that?' must be answerable. Freshness and citations are RAG's two decisive advantages — neither fine-tuning nor long-context gives you a live, auditable source.
subtopics.example:
# corpus updates constantly -> just re-index, no retraining
vector_store.upsert(new_docs)         # cheap, instant freshness

chunks = vector_store.search(query, k=5)
answer = llm(build_prompt(chunks, query))
# every claim is traceable: 'Refunds take 5 days [doc_42]'
# RAG when knowledge is big, changing, or must be cited

subtopics.title: When fine-tuning wins: style, format, and behavior
subtopics.explanation: Fine-tuning bakes patterns into the weights, so it's the right tool when you need consistent tone, a rigid output schema, a domain vocabulary, or a behavior that's hard to specify with a prompt. It teaches the model how to respond, not new facts — and it can't stay fresh without retraining, so it's a poor fit for volatile knowledge. Reach for fine-tuning when the requirement is a durable way of behaving rather than access to changing information.
subtopics.example:
# fine-tune on many (input, ideal_output) pairs to lock in a style
examples = [
    {"input": "summarize ticket", "output": "<one-line, formal, no emoji>"},
    # ...thousands more capturing the exact desired behavior
]
# after fine-tuning, the model DEFAULTS to this format without prompting
# best for HOW to respond (tone, schema) -- not for WHAT facts to know

subtopics.title: When long-context wins: a small, stable corpus that fits
subtopics.explanation: If your entire relevant corpus comfortably fits the context window and rarely changes, you can skip retrieval and paste it all in — no index, no retrieval errors, and the model sees everything at once. The catch is cost and latency scale with tokens, and quality degrades when the window is stuffed with mostly-irrelevant text, so it's for small stable bodies of knowledge, not a substitute for RAG at scale. Long-context is the simplest option precisely when the corpus is small enough to make retrieval unnecessary.
subtopics.example:
SMALL_CORPUS = load("company_handbook.md")   # ~30k tokens, rarely changes

# no retrieval step -- the whole thing goes in the prompt
prompt = f"Handbook:\n{SMALL_CORPUS}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
answer = llm(prompt)
# simplest possible design WHEN it fits; falls apart as the corpus grows

subtopics.title: They combine — it's not either/or
subtopics.explanation: The techniques stack: fine-tune a model on your format and tone, then use RAG to feed it fresh facts, and optionally give retrieved chunks a large window so more context fits per call. A common production shape is 'fine-tuned behavior + RAG knowledge', getting durable style and live, citable facts at once. Treating them as combinable rather than mutually exclusive is what unlocks the strongest designs — the decision framework picks emphasis, not a single winner.
subtopics.example:
# fine-tuned model owns the HOW; RAG supplies the WHAT
model = fine_tuned_model("support-tone-v3")   # style/format baked in
chunks = vector_store.search(query, k=5)       # fresh, citable knowledge
answer = model(build_prompt(chunks, query))
# behavior from fine-tuning + facts from RAG -> best of both

foundations.overview: RAG, fine-tuning, and long-context are three ways to get an LLM to do what you need, and the most common early mistake is treating them as interchangeable. They operate on different axes. RAG changes what the model sees: it retrieves relevant passages at query time and puts them in the prompt, so knowledge lives in an index you can update instantly and every answer can cite its source. Fine-tuning changes how the model behaves: it adjusts the weights on example input/output pairs, baking in tone, output format, and domain behavior that are hard to prompt for — but it teaches patterns, not fresh facts, and staying current means retraining. Long-context changes how much the model reads: if the entire relevant corpus fits the window, you paste it all in and skip retrieval entirely, trading token cost and latency for simplicity. The decision framework follows the need: freshness or citations point to RAG; consistent style or format points to fine-tuning; a small, stable corpus that fits points to long-context. Crucially they combine — a fine-tuned model for behavior plus RAG for knowledge is a standard production pattern — so the framework chooses emphasis and combination, not a single winner.
foundations.formalDefinition: Given a knowledge/behavior requirement, RAG augments the prompt at inference with retrieved documents (knowledge external, updatable, citable); fine-tuning updates model parameters on task examples (behavior internal, static until retrained); long-context places the full corpus in the prompt (no retrieval, cost/latency scaling with tokens). The selection is a mapping from requirement dimensions — freshness, attributability, corpus size, behavioral consistency — to one or a combination of these techniques.
foundations.whyItMatters: Choosing the wrong lever wastes effort and produces brittle systems: fine-tuning to teach facts yields a model that's confidently out of date, RAG to enforce tone underperforms a quick fine-tune, and long-context at corpus scale is slow and expensive. A clear decision framework turns 'which do we use?' from a guess into a requirement-driven choice, and reveals when to combine them.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of hiring help for a library. RAG is giving the assistant a live catalog to look things up in — always current, and they can tell you which book a fact came from. Fine-tuning is training the assistant's habits — how they write and format answers — which sticks but doesn't update itself. Long-context is just handing them the one short binder that contains everything, so they don't need a catalog at all. You pick based on whether the problem is the catalog, the habits, or the binder's size — and often you train the habits and give the catalog.
foundations.realWorldUsage: RAG for knowledge bases, docs assistants, and anything needing citations or freshness; fine-tuning for consistent brand voice, strict JSON/schema output, and classification/style tasks; long-context for reasoning over a single long document or a small fixed policy set; and the combination — fine-tuned behavior plus RAG knowledge — across most mature assistant products.
commonUseCases: RAG: large, changing, or citable knowledge bases
Fine-tune: consistent tone, rigid output format, domain behavior
Long-context: a small, stable corpus that fits the window
Combined: fine-tuned behavior + RAG for fresh, citable facts

commonMisconceptions.myth: Fine-tuning is how you add knowledge to a model.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Fine-tuning teaches behavior and patterns, not reliable up-to-date facts — it can't stay fresh without retraining and doesn't give citations. For changing or citable knowledge, use RAG.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Long context windows make RAG obsolete.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Long-context works only when the whole corpus fits and is stable; at scale it's slow, costly, and quality drops as the window fills with irrelevant text. RAG retrieves just the relevant slice and cites it.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You must pick exactly one of the three.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They combine. A standard production design fine-tunes the model for tone/format and uses RAG for fresh, citable facts — the framework picks emphasis and combination, not a single winner.

interactiveWidget.title: A decision framework for RAG vs fine-tune vs long-context
interactiveWidget.caption: Match the technique to the dominant requirement — and remember the three combine rather than compete.

config.note:
Ask what the problem actually is.

- Is the knowledge large, changing, or must it be cited? -> RAG. You update an index instead of retraining, and every answer points at its source.

- Is the need a consistent style, tone, or rigid output format (a way of BEHAVING, not new facts)? -> Fine-tune. It bakes patterns into the weights but can't stay fresh without retraining.

- Does the ENTIRE relevant corpus fit the context window and rarely change? -> Long-context. Paste it all in, skip retrieval — but cost and latency scale with tokens and quality drops as the window fills with noise.

Then combine: a fine-tuned model owns HOW to respond (tone, schema) while RAG supplies WHAT is true right now (fresh, citable facts). The framework chooses emphasis, not a single winner.

checkpoints.prompt: Your company policy documents change weekly and answers must cite the exact policy. Which technique fits best?
options: Fine-tune the model on the policies
RAG over an index of the policies
Long-context with all policies in every prompt
checkpoints.explanation: Weekly changes and citation requirements are RAG's two decisive strengths: you re-index instead of retraining for freshness, and each answer points at the retrieved chunk. Fine-tuning would go stale and can't cite; long-context may not fit and still can't update cheaply.

checkpoints.prompt: You need every response in a strict internal JSON schema and a specific formal tone, over knowledge that never changes. Which is the best primary lever?
checkpoints.explanation: A durable way of behaving — consistent format and tone — is exactly what fine-tuning bakes into the weights. RAG changes what the model sees, not how it formats, so it's the wrong lever for a pure style/format requirement.

checkpoints.prompt: Which statement about combining the techniques is correct?
options: They are mutually exclusive; pick one
You can fine-tune a model for tone/format and use RAG to supply fresh, citable facts
Long-context and RAG can never be used together
Fine-tuning removes the need for any prompt
checkpoints.explanation: The techniques stack. A common production shape is fine-tuned behavior (how to respond) plus RAG knowledge (what is true now), and retrieved chunks can ride in a large window. The framework selects emphasis and combination, not a single winner.

keyTakeaways: Three levers on different axes: RAG changes what the model sees, fine-tuning changes how it behaves, long-context changes how much it reads.
Use RAG for large, changing, or citable knowledge — you re-index instead of retraining and every answer can cite its source.
Use fine-tuning for consistent style, format, and behavior — it bakes patterns into the weights but can't stay fresh without retraining.
Use long-context for a small, stable corpus that fits the window; it's simplest there but scales poorly in cost, latency, and quality.
They combine — fine-tuned behavior plus RAG knowledge is a standard design — so match the technique to the need rather than picking a single winner.
